1 سَبَكَ , (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) aor.
سَبِكَ , (S, K,) so says El-Fárábee, and so in the Jm, and in the handwriting of Aboo-Sahl El-Harawee, (TA,) or
سَبُكَ , (Msb,) thus in the handwriting of Az, (TA,) inf. n. سَبْكٌ, (S, Mgh, Msb,) He melted, (S, Mgh, Msb, K, TA,) and cleared of its dross, (Mgh,) and poured forth (K, TA) into a mould, (TA,) gold, (Mgh, Msb, TA,) or silver, (S, Mgh, TA,) &c.; (S, TA;) and ↓ سبّك signifies the same, (K,) inf. n. تَسْبِيكٌ; (TA;) this inf. n. and سَبْكٌ both signifying the melting of gold and silver, and pouring it forth into a مِسْبَكَة [or mould] of iron, like the half of a cane divided lengthwise. (Lth, TA.) ―
-b2- Hence, سَبْكٌ is metaphorically used in the sense of تَجْرِبَةٌ. (Har pp. 140 and 211.) One says, فُلَانٌ سَبَكَتْهُ التَّجَارِبُ (tropical:) [Such a one, tryings tried, or have tried, him]. (TA.) And كَلَامٌ لَا يَثْبُتُ عَلَى السَّبْكِ is another tropical phrase [app. meaning (tropical:) Speech or language, that does not stand good, or is not sound, or valid, when tried, or tested; that will not stand trying, or testing]. (TA.)
From An Arabic-English Lexicon (Edward William Lane)
